Sally: Hey V. My week was so depressing! I talked to a few environmentalists who are raising awareness about climate change. They told me how the pesticides that have been released into the water by chemical companies are actually causing irreparable damage to the environment.
Vanessa: That sounds terrible! Do you know what we can do to avoid this disaster?
Sally: We should stop wasting so many resources. If we don't change our behavior immediately, many species of wildlife will face extinction.

Vanessa: I read about some programs that tackle this problem. I joined a group of restaurant owners and managers who stopped buying meat that was produced by farms releasing high levels of pollutants.
Sally: More people should know about the food that they eat.
Vanessa: Yeah. If people read the labels, they would stop buying certain products. If I spent less time at the restaurant, I would feel more involved with the problems which we're facing globally. Maybe I should get out more.

Sally: Trust me, if you knew about weather patterns the way I do now, you wouldn't want to go outside!
Vanessa: Can you tell me what I should do to make a difference?
Sally: No idea! I was asked the same question by many of my readers this week. I should come up with an answer, I guess.

Discussing How to Deal With Problems

When you want to offer advice or give solutions to a problem, you use modals like might, should or could.

You use the first conditional sentences with If clauses to talk about real possibilities in the future.

You use the second conditional to talk about unreal or imaginary (hypothetical) situations in the future.
The modals can go at the beginning of the sentence, or after a clause starting with “If ...”

Example:
If ... , I would/I wouldn't ...
If ... , you could / should ...
You use the First Conditional to say it's possible that you will do or not do something. In that condition, something else may, will or will not happen.
The parts of the sentence are divided into two clauses: the If clause and the Condition clause.
You use the Second Conditional to talk about hypothetical situations. It's not certain that it's possible to fulfill the condition.

Example:
If I had a million dollars, I would buy a car.

Do you have a million dollars? No.
Is it possible to suddenly get a million dollars? Not really.
What would you do if you had a million dollars? Buy a car.
You use the Simple Past verb + would
If we don't change our behavior immediately, many species of wildlife will face extinction.
If people read the labels, they would stop buying certain products.
If I spent less time at the restaurant, I would feel more involved with environmental issues.
There are several ways to ask for help or advice in English. You can use polite and casual language to do this. Let's look at one particular structure for asking for help or advice.

You can use the structure:
Can / Could / Do + you + verb + me (optional) + question word

Example:
Do you know what we can do to avoid this disaster?
Can you tell me what I should do to make a difference?
These questions are often used in interviews. You ask this type of questions when you want to know more about a topic.
